audit.how.d: A break is a year when the source mix shifts (total variation ≥ 0.5). A four-fold jump in the count is also a break, and so is coverage starting or stopping. The same goes for a Pettitt step that lines up with a catalog-wide break. We keep the longest span with no break (at least {years} years, {mean}+ events a year). We test only that span, with Mann-Kendall and Theil-Sen.
audit.lead: EONET lists the natural events that its partner sources report. Sources joined and left over the years. So a rising count can mean a growing catalog, not a changing planet. We audit every category for catalog breaks before we test any trend.

gloss.break.d: A year when the event list itself changed. Its mix of sources shifted, or its count suddenly rose or fell.
gloss.ci.d: The speeds of change that fit the data. Ranges built this way miss the true speed only rarely.
gloss.merra.d: A NASA model that rebuilds past weather across the whole planet. Measurements from satellites, stations, balloons and aircraft guide it.
gloss.mk.d: Compares each year with every later year, counting rises and falls. Far more of one kind shows a direction.
gloss.ndvi.d: A satellite index of how green and dense vegetation is. On land, it goes from near 0 (bare ground) to about 0.9 (dense forest).
gloss.p.d: The chance of seeing a trend at least this strong if there were no real trend.
gloss.pct.d: The percent of earlier years here that had a lower value than this one. Near either end means unusual.
gloss.reanalysis.d: A NASA model constrained by millions of observations, giving consistent data everywhere, every day since 1980.
gloss.sen.d: The typical speed of change, robust to outliers.
gloss.sig.d: Unlikely to be produced by random variation alone. It does not mean large or important.
gloss.span.d: The longest stretch with no change in how the event list was built. Only those years are tested.
gloss.theilsen.d: The middle value of the change per year, measured between every pair of years. One odd year cannot drag it.
gloss.trend.d: A change that keeps the same direction over many years.
gloss.verdict.d: Confirmed: random year-to-year ups and downs would rarely make a pattern this strong. Inconclusive: it could be chance.
gloss.z.d: How many usual swings this value is above or below the average of earlier years.

method.anom.d: For each natural event in EONET, we take the {days} days before it was first reported. We compare them with the same calendar window in every year since 1981, using NASA POWER daily data. We check daily high, rainfall and soil wetness, and keep the most unusual. A record or a value outside the most extreme 2.5 % on either side counts as anomalous.
method.audit.d: Before counting events, we look for years when the catalog itself changed. Signs of a change: new sources join, volume jumps four-fold, coverage starts or stops. We only test a trend inside the longest stretch with none of those breaks, at least 8 years long.

method.lead: Nature is noisy. A few warm years do not make a warming trend. One record month does not make a disaster. A longer list of events can just mean more people are counting. We use three tests, one for each kind of evidence.
method.lead.short: Nature is noisy. Here is how we tell a real change from chance, in five steps.
method.limits.d: A point value represents a grid cell of about 50 km (MERRA-2) or a 2 × 2 km box (MODIS). Consecutive years can be correlated, which makes p-values look smaller than they are. A significant trend tells us something changed, not why: the “Why” sections cite the leading scientific explanations.

method.s1.d: Summer and winter would look like a trend. We use one value per year: the yearly mean, or the mean of the growing season for vegetation.
method.s2.d: Mann-Kendall compares every year with every later year. If later years are higher far more often than lower, the series has a direction.
method.s3.d: Theil-Sen takes the median of the slopes between all pairs of years. One extreme year cannot drag it.
method.s4.d: We check how often random year-to-year noise would produce this pattern. If it is less than 5 % of the time (p < 0.05), we call the trend significant.

st1.d: NASA's Terra satellite and the MERRA-2 reanalysis record the planet every day.
st1.how: MODIS on Terra sees vegetation at 250 m. MERRA-2 combines millions of observations with a physics model. It gives temperature, rain and soil water everywhere since 1980.
st2.d: Public NASA services, no login: POWER, ORNL DAAC, EONET and GIBS.
st2.how: An open Python script (scripts/build_cases.py) downloads every series and stores it with the case file. Anyone can run it again and get the same numbers.
st3.d: One value per year, so the seasons don't look like a trend.
st3.how: The yearly mean for climate variables. For vegetation, the mean of the growing season: June–September in the Amazon, July–August in the Arctic.
st4.d: Mann-Kendall for the direction, Theil-Sen for the speed, a 95 % band for the uncertainty.
st4.how: Both tools are non-parametric: they don't assume a bell curve, and one extreme year cannot fool them.
st5.d: Strong, moderate or weak evidence, written in plain words.
st5.how: p < 0.01 is strong, p < 0.05 moderate, anything else weak. Weak means “not proven”, never “no change”.

tour.ask.1.d: Start with the topic: heat, rain, vegetation… Only the topics NASA data can answer appear.
tour.ask.2.d: Whether it changed over the years, was unusual before an event, changes alike in two places, or whether there are more events than before.
tour.ask.2.t: What do you want to know?
tour.ask.3.d: Pick a reviewed place or event. Each one has its data ready to test.
tour.ask.4.d: Here you see your full question. Once the three pieces are set, the button takes you to investigate it.
tour.ask.5.d: Tap an example and the three pieces fill in for you.
tour.briefing.1.d: How many trends were confirmed, how many events came after unusual weeks, and how many categories really changed. Tap a figure to see those cases.
tour.briefing.2.d: Three ways to start: open a case file, pick a place on the globe, or learn not to be fooled.
tour.briefing.3.d: The same variable can rise in one place and fall in another. That is why each place is tested on its own.
tour.briefing.4.d: More events counted are not always more disasters. Sometimes what changed was the list, not the planet.
tour.briefing.5.d: Trends already investigated, each with its verdict. Open the one you like to read its case file.
tour.briefing.6.d: Go into the case files and pick the case that intrigues you most.
tour.case.1.d: The essentials come first, in plain words. The exact figures sit below, in case you want them.
tour.case.2.d: The verdict says how clear the evidence is. It does not say whether something rises or falls, or how serious it is.
tour.case.3.d: The figure says how much and, when it has an arrow, which way. The note beside it explains what it measures.
tour.case.4.d: Here is the evidence. The scale says how clear it is, not how big the change is.
tour.case.5.d: The limits of this case, said plainly. It does not predict the future, explain why it happened, or tell you what to do.
tour.case.6.d: Copy the sentence, the citation with its source, or the link, to use this case wherever you need.
tour.cases.1.d: Type “rain”, “wildfire” or the name of a city, without the country. With a place, cases are sorted from nearest to farthest.
tour.cases.1.t: Search a topic or a place
tour.cases.2.d: Heat, rain, vegetation, disasters… Each topic shows how many cases it has.
tour.cases.3.d: Here you see how many cases are shown and which filters are on. Tap a filter's ✕ to remove it.
tour.cases.4.d: On top, what was investigated and where; below, its verdict. Open it to read the full case file.
tour.cases.5.d: This checks whether there really are more events or just more being counted. Sometimes the list changed, not the planet.
tour.compare.1.d: The same variable and the same method in two places. Each place has its own test; nothing is mixed.
tour.compare.2.d: One can be confirmed and the other not. It is not a contradiction: they are different places.
tour.compare.3.d: This note puts the two directions side by side and says whether they change alike.
tour.compare.4.d: Comparing does not explain why they change differently, nor predict what will happen.
tour.compare.5.d: Pick the places again, or ask a new question.
tour.data.1.d: Choose what to see: region, variable, type or dates. The filters stay in the link, so you can share the view.
tour.data.2.d: The main figures of what you filtered.
tour.data.3.d: The stored data, row by row. If the table is wide, slide it sideways.
tour.explore.1.d: Drag the globe to spin it, and tap any point to see what we know there. These buttons zoom in, zoom out or bring back the whole planet.
tour.explore.2.d: Tap here to explore by region, or type a case file or a storm, and the globe flies there.
tour.explore.3.d: Case files shows the pins; Events, what NASA logged; Weather, conditions live; and Data, figures on the map.
tour.explore.4.d: This shows what you picked on the globe. Close it with the ✕ or with Esc.
tour.explore.wait.d: Once the Earth appears, tap “How does this page work?” again and we will show you each control.
tour.home.1.d: Here you investigate the Earth with public NASA data. You don't need to know any science to start.
tour.home.10.d: Search solved cases by topic or place, or press /. To investigate something new, start at “I have a question”.
tour.home.11.d: Switch the language here, and pick the light or dark theme.
tour.home.2.d: Pick a topic and a place. We walk you through it, step by step, to the verdict.
tour.home.3.d: Spin the globe, read case files already solved, or see how we test the data.
tour.home.4.d: Trend: a change that lasts decades. Anomaly: a few weeks far from normal. Event: something NASA logged at a place and a date.
tour.home.5.d: Sometimes the data are not enough to claim anything. “Inconclusive” is an answer too.
tour.home.6.d: From here you reach every section: ask, briefing, case files, the globe and how we know. The page you are on stays marked.
tour.home.7.d: These five tabs take you to Home, Ask, Case Files, the globe and How we know. The one you are on stays marked.
tour.home.8.d: The bar counts how many case files you opened. The arrow unfolds the three kinds: trends, anomalies and audit.
tour.home.9.d: The case files you opened recently stay here, so you can get back to them quickly.
tour.lesson-check.1.d: Years always go up and down a little. The question is whether the line goes beyond that swing.
tour.lesson-check.2.d: Choose whether you see a clear direction, or whether it could be just the year-to-year swing.
tour.lesson-check.3.d: The test measures how often pure chance would make a pattern like this. The rarer, the clearer the evidence.
tour.lesson-check.4.d: Go back, move on or, if you have not answered yet, skip the question. Your answer does not change the result: it only helps you think.
tour.lesson-done.1.d: What you thought and what the test found, side by side. It does not matter if they match: that is how you investigate.
tour.lesson-done.2.d: Try the question that goes with this one, or the same one in another place.
tour.lesson-done.3.d: Open the full case file, download the data, see it on the globe, or read how we tested it.
tour.lesson-done.4.d: Here are the sources, so you can repeat the test on your own.
tour.lesson-guess.1.d: Look at how the dots move over the years. The line appears once you say what you see.
tour.lesson-guess.2.d: Is it going up, going down, or can't you tell yet? There is no wrong answer: it is your first idea.
tour.lesson-guess.3.d: The line sums up where the dots are heading, and the figure says how much it changes per decade.
tour.lesson-guess.4.d: Go back, move on or, if you have not answered yet, skip the question. Your answer does not change the result: it only helps you think.
tour.lesson-look.1.d: The bar shows where you are in the investigation and how far the verdict is.
tour.lesson-look.2.d: Under “Aa” you pick Simple, Guided or Scientific. It changes how much is explained, never the figures.
tour.lesson-look.3.d: The place, the variable, how each year is summed up, the period and the source. It is all the test will use.
tour.lesson-look.4.d: Each value describes a square about 50 km wide, not a whole country or a thermometer at someone's door.
tour.lesson-look.5.d: Go back or move on here whenever you want. The ✕ at the top takes you out.
tour.lesson-verdict.1.d: The stamp says whether the change is clear or could be chance. The bar says how strong the evidence is.
tour.lesson-verdict.2.d: A sentence you can repeat or copy, with its source.
tour.lesson-verdict.3.d: This is where you read how much it changed and which way. The stamp above does not: it only says how clear the test is.
tour.lesson-verdict.4.d: It does not predict the future, explain the cause, or tell you what to do.
tour.lesson-verdict.5.d: It comes from published science. This test does not prove it: it only measures whether there was a change.
tour.method.1.d: Jump straight to the part you are interested in.
tour.method.2.d: The steps we follow with every case, always in the same order and with the same test.
tour.method.3.d: The more things you check, the easier a false alarm gets. Try it yourself in this lab.
tour.method.4.d: Move the noise and the trend, and see when the test can spot it and when it cannot.
tour.method.5.d: Where the data come from, and what each technical word means.
tour.method.6.d: What this method cannot say, said plainly.
